cf.title: [RFC PATCH v1] On-demand WAL replay: accept connections before crash recovery has applied the WAL

input.subject: [RFC PATCH v1] On-demand WAL replay: accept connections before crash recovery has applied the WAL

verdict_reasoning: The goal is stated and measured, but the design leaves the pending window undefined in several places. No checkpoint can complete during the drain and nothing bounds pg_wal growth (replication-ondisk-1). The proposal does not cover a redo PANIC in a backend (replication-ondisk-2), and nothing checks the new rules for redo routines (maintenance-fit-1). The simpler unwaited-checkpoint path is not compared (already-exists-1). All are fixable, and the thread has only the author's message.

brief.title: On-demand WAL replay so the server accepts connections before crash recovery ends
brief.problem: After a crash the server refuses connections until it has replayed all WAL since the last checkpoint and finished the end-of-recovery checkpoint. Both costs grow with WAL volume, so downtime after a crash grows with it. The target is any operator who wants to cut that downtime.
brief.proposed_design: With fast_crash_recovery on, the startup process applies only records without block references and stores, per page, the LSNs of page-modifying records in a dshash table in DSM. The server then opens, and a page is replayed inside StartReadBuffersImpl() under BM_IO_IN_PROGRESS on its first read from disk. A new auxiliary process replays the remaining pages, then drops the index and requests a checkpoint.
user_visible_surface: New GUC fast_crash_recovery (boolean, default off, server start only).
New auxiliary process type "fast recovery worker" (log/backend type fastrecoveryworker).
New wait event FAST_RECOVERY_DRAIN and new LWLocks/tranches LSNIndex, LSNIndexDSA, LSNIndexHash.
Until the worker finishes, CHECKPOINT, pg_backup_start() and CREATE/DROP DATABASE fail with "checkpoint request failed", and clean shutdown waits.
Expected output of the stats regression test changes, likely new pg_stat_io rows for the new process type.
author_claims: Time to accept connections drops 1.9x to 5.5x in pgbench crash tests on a 6-vCPU VM, with the best case at full_page_writes = off.
The first full scan of a hot table after opening is about 1.5 to 7 times slower, and the background drain costs more total time than stock recovery.
Checks with per-table hashes, the tpcb balance invariant and pg_amcheck --heapallindexed found no differences against stock recovery.
check-world passes with the setting forced on, except 018_wal_optimize, which can fail because it issues CHECKPOINT right after a crash restart.
The design adds nothing new to the buffer manager protocol, and an exclusive lock can replace a cleanup lock because no backend can hold the page yet.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted; message #2 is a forward of message #1. No reviewer has replied, and CFbot reports that the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: The proposal does not say what happens if the DSM index cannot be allocated or fills /dev/shm, as it has no cap yet.
The proposal does not say what happens on a second crash while pages are still pending, or whether the next recovery rebuilds the index from the same WAL.
The proposal does not say how a page that fails replay repeatedly is reported, or whether it blocks every reader of that page.
The proposal does not say how long WAL segments are kept, or whether WAL recycling and archiving wait for the worker.
The proposal does not say how pg_rewind, pg_basebackup, replicas and logical decoding behave during the pending window.
The proposal does not say how a user can see progress of the drain, since no view or counter is listed.

prior_attempts.title: Add DB_IN_END_OF_RECOVERY_CHECKPOINT state for control file
prior_attempts.quote: This patch would bring some extra visibility for something that's not incorrect either on HEAD, as end-of-recovery checkpoints are the same things as shutdown checkpoints.
prior_attempts.reason: Michael Paquier argued that the current state is not incorrect, because an end-of-recovery checkpoint is a shutdown checkpoint and the code has relied on that for about 10 years. He said the change was not checked against other assumptions, such as unlogged relation reset needing a clean shutdown, and that it leaves an invalid minimum recovery point in DB_IN_ARCHIVE_RECOVERY. He added that it would make back-patching harder in a sensitive area, and the entry was closed after the thread went quiet.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P14 changed the control file state around the end-of-recovery checkpoint. This proposal opens the server before any such checkpoint, so code that treats it as a shutdown checkpoint is affected.

objections.title: No checkpoint during the drain lets pg_wal and the redo window grow
objections.failure_scenario: A busy primary reopens after a crash and takes full write load while the worker drains for minutes. With CreateCheckPoint() refused, max_wal_size is not honoured and pg_wal can fill the disk, causing a PANIC. Any second crash replays from the old redo point, through all old and new WAL.
objections.argument: Message #1 refuses checkpoints until the LSN index is gone, and case C shows a 507 s drain on an idle server. Under load, the worker competes with clients, so the window has no stated upper bound. The proposal has no limit on WAL kept, no cap on drain time, and no fallback that forces a checkpoint. [P9] was reverted because committed changes stayed un-checkpointed with full reliance on the WAL stream, and this design creates the same state after every crash.
objections.author_must_show: What bounds pg_wal growth and the redo window while the worker drains under write load, and what happens when that bound is reached?

precedents.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"

critic.reasoning: CreateCheckPoint() refuses while the index exists, and the proposal gives no bound on pg_wal growth or on the drain under write load. [P9] was about an idle server with no end to the gap, so it must not be used as support.

objections.title: Redo errors in backends can turn into a crash-restart loop
objections.failure_scenario: One page has a record whose redo hits a PANIC-level consistency check. In stock recovery, startup stops once with a clear message. Here the server opens, the first reader of that page triggers a cluster-wide crash restart, recovery reopens, and the next reader of the page crashes it again, each time over more WAL.
objections.argument: Many redo routines report inconsistent pages with PANIC, and the commit message covers only ERROR and FATAL cleanup in a backend. Moving redo into ordinary backends and the worker means a redo PANIC now resets all of shared memory, including the DSM index, while clients are connected. The proposal does not say how a page that fails replay is reported, isolated, or kept from restarting the cluster again and again.
objections.author_must_show: What happens when on-demand redo of one page raises PANIC, and how does the design stop repeated crash restarts over a growing WAL window?

critic.reasoning: Core redo routines do raise PANIC on inconsistent pages, and a PANIC in a backend triggers a crash restart. The commit message covers only ERROR and FATAL cleanup, so nothing stops the next reader of that page from repeating the crash.

objections.title: Every redo routine, including custom rmgrs, gains unchecked new rules
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch, or an extension using a custom WAL resource manager, adds a redo routine that reads a second page or assumes all blocks of a record are applied together. With fast_crash_recovery on, that page is replayed wrongly or nests replay. The damage shows up after some production crash, as silent page corruption.
objections.argument: Message #1 makes correctness depend on new rules: redo of an indexed page never reads another indexed page, other blocks report BLK_DONE, initialized blocks go to a scratch local buffer, and an exclusive lock stands in for a cleanup lock. These hold for today's core redo routines by inspection, but nothing in the design checks them. The default is off and only crash tests exercise the feature, so a routine that breaks a rule passes check-world. Custom rmgrs are outside the project's control.
objections.author_must_show: What check, assertion or test fails when a new or extension redo routine breaks the one-page, no-nesting rule this design depends on?

critic.reasoning: The BLK_DONE handling is already required of redo routines, but the rule that redo of an indexed page reads no other page is new and unchecked. An assertion, or eager replay for custom rmgrs, could fix it in a later version, so it is fixable.

objections.title: The existing promotion path already skips the waited end-of-recovery checkpoint
objections.failure_scenario: An operator enables fast_crash_recovery and gets a deferred-replay buffer manager path and a new auxiliary process. Most of their downtime was the end-of-recovery checkpoint. Writing an end-of-recovery record and requesting the checkpoint without waiting, as promotion already does, would have removed that part with far less new state.
objections.argument: In case A the checkpoint is 9.2 of 15.1 s, and in B it is 30.4 of 96.1 s. Postgres already ends archive recovery at promotion with an end-of-recovery record and an unwaited checkpoint. The proposal does not compare against reusing that path for crash recovery. Only the gain beyond that simpler change justifies replay inside StartReadBuffersImpl() and the failing CHECKPOINT window.
objections.author_must_show: How much time to accept connections remains if crash recovery only ends with an end-of-recovery record and an unwaited checkpoint, and does that remainder justify on-demand page replay?

critic.reasoning: The tables already split redo from checkpoint time, and stock redo alone is 5.8 s against 2.7 s in A and 173 s against 106 s in C. The proposal does not discuss the simpler unwaited-checkpoint path, so the design comparison is still open.

objections.title: CHECKPOINT, backups and CREATE DATABASE fail after restart with the GUC on
objections.failure_scenario: After a crash, a backup tool calls pg_backup_start() or pg_basebackup, or a deployment script runs CREATE DATABASE. Each gets "checkpoint request failed" for as long as the drain runs, which was over 8 minutes in run C. The operator finds out when the nightly backup or a provisioning job fails, with an error that does not name the cause.
objections.argument: With the GUC on, commands that work on every server today fail for an unbounded time after a crash. The GUC changes the semantics of user commands, beyond recovery timing. Message #1, item 4, leaves the choice between failing and waiting open and ships the error in v1. The project's own 018_wal_optimize test already trips on this, which suggests external scripts will too. A committer would likely ask for one defined contract and a specific error message before the GUC is exposed.
objections.author_must_show: Will CHECKPOINT, pg_backup_start() and CREATE/DROP DATABASE wait during the drain, and if they fail, what errcode and hint tell the operator why and for how long?

critic.reasoning: Message #1, item 4, raises this itself and leaves the choice open, so v1 has no settled contract. The error text "checkpoint request failed" does not name the cause, and 018_wal_optimize already fails on it.

other_surviving.title: Clean shutdown can block for minutes, beyond service manager stop timeouts
other_surviving.failure_scenario: After fast crash recovery, an operator restarts the server for a config change. The clean shutdown waits for the worker, which took 507 s in run C. pg_ctl stop gives up after its default 60 s wait, and a service manager stop timeout sends SIGKILL. The result is another crash recovery and an operator who cannot see why the stop hung.
other_surviving.argument: pg_ctl, systemd units and HA tools such as Patroni assume a fast or smart shutdown finishes in bounded time once clients leave. The proposal makes shutdown time depend on the remaining drain work, and it offers no view or counter to show progress. Message #1 states that shutdown waits but does not say what fast or immediate mode does during the window, or whether an immediate stop restarts the indexing from the same WAL.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What do smart, fast and immediate shutdown each do while pages are pending, and how can an operator see how much drain work is left?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says a clean shutdown waits for the worker, and case C shows a 507 s drain against the 60 s default wait of pg_ctl. The proposal does not say what fast or immediate shutdown does while pages are pending.

other_surviving.title: Pending-recovery window is not visible to clients or tools
other_surviving.failure_scenario: Monitoring and failover tools see accepted connections and pg_is_in_recovery() = false, so they mark the node healthy and send full traffic. Queries then run 1.5 to 7 times slower, and checkpoint-dependent tasks fail. Nothing in SQL tells the tool that the server is still in a degraded post-crash state.
other_surviving.argument: Today, accepting connections with pg_is_in_recovery() false means recovery is done and the end-of-recovery checkpoint exists. The proposal adds a third state with user-visible consequences, but it exposes this state only through a process in pg_stat_activity and one wait event. Existing interfaces such as pg_stat_progress_* views, a function, or a control file state would follow established practice for long background work.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which SQL-visible signal, such as a function, progress view or pg_controldata field, lets tools detect the pending window and its progress?

critic.reasoning: The patch lists a process type, one wait event and three LWLocks, but no function, view or counter for the pending window. The slowdown applies to first reads only, but tools still cannot detect the state or its progress.

other_surviving.title: One all-or-nothing patch in bufmgr and recovery with no reviewer
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the 94 KB patch, and a bug appears in StartReadBuffersImpl() or in redo after a crash a year later. The committer must debug buffer manager, checkpointer and recovery interactions alone. The bug list in message #1 shows how subtle these bugs are.
other_surviving.argument: 0001 holds the whole feature, so nothing can be committed or tested in production before the rest. The WAL-segment posix_fadvise or the redo-routine rules could have gone in as separate patches. Message #1 lists five crash classes found during development, all of the form "the page was visible before it was current". No committer who knows bufmgr or xlogrecovery has replied, and the patch has no measurement of the read-path cost with the setting off.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which parts could be committed first on their own, and what does the extra check in StartReadBuffersImpl() cost when the setting is off?

critic.reasoning: 0001 holds the whole feature, and the thread has no measurement of the StartReadBuffersImpl() cost with the setting off. The lack of a reviewer one month into an RFC belongs under committability and does not count against the design.

other_surviving.title: No field evidence that crash-restart downtime is a pressing user problem
other_surviving.failure_scenario: The project accepts a large change to the buffer manager read path and to redo, then finds few deployments enable it. Operators who care most about downtime fail over to a standby, where the feature does not apply. Single-node operators can already bound recovery time with checkpoint_timeout and max_wal_size.
other_surviving.argument: The only evidence of demand is the author's pgbench harness on one VM (message #1); it cites no field reports, no -general or -bugs threads, and no other database with this feature. Scenarios A to D use crash windows of 2 to 10 GB with no checkpoint during the workload, which is a configuration choice. The patch excludes archive recovery and standby mode, which narrows the group to single-node crash restarts. No other person has posted.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which production deployments wait minutes for crash recovery today, why can they neither fail over nor shorten checkpoint_timeout, and how many such reports exist?

critic.reasoning: The thread has one poster and cites no field reports, and the patch excludes standby and archive recovery. This is a request to show demand and does not count against the idea itself.

refuted.title: No checkpoint can complete during the drain window
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator turns on fast_crash_recovery on a busy server, and after a crash the drain runs for minutes (506 s in case C). New WAL piles up next to the old window because no checkpoint can complete, and pg_backup_start() fails. A second crash in that window replays all of it from the old redo point.
refuted.argument: [P9] was reverted because leaving committed changes un-checkpointed makes the server rely on the WAL stream alone. This proposal does that on purpose for the whole drain, and CreateCheckPoint() refuses while the index exists (message #1). Message #1 measures the drain but does not say how WAL retention, archiving or a second crash behave in that window. A committer would likely ask for a bound on the window, or a way for checkpoints to work during it.
refuted.author_must_show: What bounds the time and WAL volume with no completed checkpoint, and what does a second crash during the drain replay?

precedents.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which states the same checkpoint gap with a more concrete failure. [P9] concerned an idle server skipping checkpoints with no end, so it is weak support here.

refuted.title: Clean shutdown after a crash restart waits for the full drain
refuted.failure_scenario: After a crash restart, an operator needs a clean stop for a planned failover or a minor-version upgrade. The stop waits for the fast recovery worker, which took 506 s in case C, so it passes the default pg_ctl wait. The operator then sends an immediate stop, which starts another crash recovery.
refuted.argument: In [P10], skipping work at the end-of-recovery checkpoint was not accepted because the cost then lands on the next shutdown or checkpoint. Here the drain costs more total time than stock recovery (message #1), and a clean shutdown waits for it. So a stop issued soon after opening can take longer than the downtime the feature saved, and message #1 does not discuss this case.
refuted.author_must_show: What happens to a clean shutdown requested during the drain, and can it end without waiting for every pending page?

precedents.title: skip replication slot snapshot/map file removal during end-of-recovery checkpoint

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. [P10] was withdrawn because it did not fix slow regular checkpoints, which is a different reason from a shutdown that waits for the drain.

refuted.title: Switchover and replica rebuild are blocked until the drain ends
refuted.failure_scenario: After a primary crash, an HA tool tries a planned switchover or rebuilds a lost standby with pg_basebackup. The clean shutdown waits for the worker, and pg_backup_start() fails with "checkpoint request failed". The tool times out and escalates to an immediate stop, which causes another crash and restarts recovery.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states that a clean shutdown waits for the worker and that pg_backup_start(), CHECKPOINT and CREATE/DROP DATABASE fail during the window, which in case C lasts over eight minutes. Replication tooling expects a clean shutdown to write a shutdown checkpoint record for standbys, and expects base backups to start, soon after the server accepts connections. The proposal does not show how these cross-node operations behave, or whether they can wait in a bounded way.
refuted.author_must_show: How do switchover, pg_basebackup and pg_rewind-based failback behave during the pending window, and is there a bounded wait instead of an error or an indefinite block?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2 for the shutdown wait and of standards-compat-1 for the pg_backup_start() failure. The HA framing adds no separate failure beyond those two.

refuted.title: No checkpoint during the drain lets WAL and second-crash recovery grow
refuted.failure_scenario: After a crash at scale, the drain runs for minutes, about 507 s in case C, while clients write at full speed. No checkpoint runs, so pg_wal cannot be recycled and can fill the disk. A second crash in that window then replays the old WAL plus everything written since, so recovery takes longer.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says CreateCheckPoint() refuses while the index exists, and the drain is serial and unbounded in time. The proposal does not say what happens to WAL recycling, archiving or a second crash during that window. [P9] was reverted because letting committed changes go un-checkpointed for an unbounded time leaves the system relying on the WAL stream alone. Here the gap starts right after a crash, when that risk matters most.
refuted.author_must_show: How large can pg_wal grow during the drain under a write-heavy load, and how long does recovery take after a second crash in that window?

precedents.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which covers pg_wal growth and the second-crash redo window with the same facts.

refuted.title: New failure modes reach backup, CREATE DATABASE and tooling
refuted.failure_scenario: An HA tool restarts the primary after a crash and right away starts a base backup or runs CREATE DATABASE for a tenant. The call fails with "checkpoint request failed" for several minutes. The operator finds out from failed automation, and no view shows when the window ends.
refuted.argument: Message #1 lists CHECKPOINT, pg_backup_start() and CREATE/DROP DATABASE as failing during the window and leaves the choice between failing and waiting open. The proposal does not say how pg_rewind, replicas or logical decoding behave, and it adds no progress view. Each tool that assumes a running primary can checkpoint must learn about this new state. The project would then have to support that state for good.
refuted.author_must_show: Which commands and external tools behave differently during the pending window, and how does an operator see when it ends?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the failing commands and of standards-compat-3 for the missing progress view.

refuted.title: Checkpoint spacing already bounds crash recovery WAL; benchmarks disable it
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator with a downtime budget already sets max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout so that recovery replays a few GiB at most. For them the measured 2 to 10 GiB windows with no checkpoint never occur. They gain much less than the numbers suggest but still carry the new failure modes.
refuted.argument: The harness runs with "No checkpoint runs during the workload", so each case replays all WAL since start. The usual way to bound recovery time is max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout. Shorter spacing costs more full-page writes in normal running, so this is a trade-off, but the proposal does not discuss it or measure at typical settings. A committer would likely ask what remains for a tuned server.
refuted.author_must_show: What is the reduction in time to accept connections with default or commonly tuned max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout, with checkpoints running during the workload?

critic.reasoning: Cases A, B and D replay 1.8 to 2.7 GiB, which is within the "few GiB" the objection grants a tuned server. A crash window of that size is the same input whether or not earlier checkpoints ran; the tuning trade-off is covered by demand-1.

refuted.title: Faster connect time is paid for by a long degraded window
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator enables the setting, the server opens about 90 seconds earlier in scenario C, and then runs for over eight minutes with slower first scans. During that window CHECKPOINT, pg_backup_start() and CREATE DATABASE fail. A backup job or migration script that runs just after restart fails, and the operator finds out from its error.
refuted.argument: Message #1 reports scenario C first scans at 72.6 s versus 10.4 s, and a 506.8 s drain, against a 93 s gain in time to accept connections. The proposal does not show that users prefer "accepting connections but slow and unable to checkpoint" over "down but fully ready". Every future redo routine must also keep the rule that redo of an indexed page reads no other page. That cost falls on all developers, while the gain goes only to sites that enable the setting.
refuted.author_must_show: Which applications benefit from accepting connections while checkpoints and backups fail and first reads are several times slower, and do their operators prefer that trade?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states the trade of more total work for earlier availability, and the setting is off by default, so the slow window falls only on sites that enable it. The failing commands and the redo rule are covered by standards-compat-1 and maintenance-fit-1.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-1: No checkpoint during the drain lets pg_wal and the redo window grow

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Page redo moves out of the startup process, and CreateCheckPoint() refuses until the fast recovery worker finishes.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Redo routines, including those of custom WAL resource managers, run under new one-page rules; bufmgr.h changes.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: CHECKPOINT, backups and CREATE DATABASE fail after restart with the GUC on

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: Adds fast_crash_recovery, a boolean set at server start, default off.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: CHECKPOINT, backups and CREATE DATABASE fail after restart with the GUC on

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: New auxiliary process, DSM index, and rules that every future redo routine must keep, across bufmgr, checkpointer and recovery.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Adds a check in StartReadBuffersImpl(), the common read path; no measurement with the setting off.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What bounds pg_wal growth and the redo window while the worker drains under write load, and what does a second crash in that window replay?
What happens when on-demand redo of one page raises PANIC in a backend, and how does the design prevent repeated crash restarts on that page?
What assertion or test fails when a new redo routine, or one in a custom resource manager, reads a second page during on-demand redo?
How much time to accept connections remains if crash recovery only writes an end-of-recovery record and requests an unwaited checkpoint, as promotion does?
Will CHECKPOINT, pg_backup_start() and CREATE/DROP DATABASE wait or fail during the drain, and what do smart, fast and immediate shutdown each do?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows both the buffer manager read path and WAL recovery with checkpoints; none has replied in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of page redo inside backends after every crash, for the new redo-routine rules, and for the checkpoint-free window, for as long as the setting exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author plans more measurements on EC2 and has a waiting variant written. CFbot has asked for a rebase since 2026-10-18 and no new version is posted.

priority.reason: A single 94 KiB patch touches bufmgr, checkpointer, postmaster and recovery, and the behaviour of the pending window is still open. The thread cites no field reports, and the feature excludes standby and archive recovery, so the size of the audience is not shown.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can confirm that no path makes a page visible before it is current, or that failed replay cleans up correctly. The cost in StartReadBuffersImpl() with the setting off is also unmeasured.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
Reverted commit(s): Remove some unstable parts from new TAP test for archive status check
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This part of the test was included originally in 4e87c48, but got
reverted as of f9c1b8d because of timing issues in the test, where,
after more analysis, we found that the standbys may not have recovered
from the archives all the segments needed by the test.  This stabilizes
the test by making sure that standbys replay up to the position returned
by pg_switch_wal(), meaning that all segments are recovered before the
manual checkpoint that tests WAL segment recycling and its interactions
with archive status files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the patch to check if we've reached end-of-backup also when doing crash recovery, and throw an error if not.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert the patch to check if we've reached end-of-backup also when doing crash recovery, and throw an error if not. hubert depesz lubaczewski pointed out that that situation also happens in the crash recovery following a system crash that happens during an online backup.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert the patch to check if we've reached end-of-backup also when doing
crash recovery, and throw an error if not. hubert depesz lubaczewski pointed
out that that situation also happens in the crash recovery following a
system crash that happens during an online backup.

We might want to do something smarter in 9.1, like put the check back for
backups taken with pg_basebackup, but that's for another patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Better fix for "unarchived WAL files get deleted on crash recovery" bug.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Better fix for "unarchived WAL files get deleted on crash recovery" bug.
Reverted commit(s): Don't delete unarchived WAL files during crash recovery.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert my earlier fix for the bug that unarchived WAL files get deleted on
crash recovery, commit c9cc7e05c6d82a9781883a016c70d95aa4923122. We create
a .done file for files streamed or restored from archive, so the WAL file
recycling logic used during normal operation works just as well during
archive recovery.

Per Fujii Masao's suggestion.

precedents_retrieved.title: postgres.exe doesn't output crash dump when it crashes before main()
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, postmaster calls SetErrorMode() to turn off Windows Error Reporting (WER), and child processes inherit that mode, so a crash before main() produces no crash dump. The patch resets the error mode for child processes and calls SetErrorMode() again at the start of main(), so WER can write a dump for early crashes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers worried that with WER on, an early crash can show a popup that blocks the process until someone closes it. This could freeze automated setups that run "pg_ctl start" outside a service, and the patch had no GUC to control it. Tom Lane judged that the patch would likely break some startup scenarios for a marginal gain in error reporting, and Michael Paquier agreed and marked the entry rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It seems very likely
that it will break some startup scenarios, and the incremental benefit
in error reporting seems marginal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reword docs of GUCs restart_after_crash and remove_temp_files_after_crash
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch rewords the docs and guc.c descriptions of restart_after_crash and remove_temp_files_after_crash, which say "backend crash". The new text lists the processes whose crash triggers the behaviour: backends, auxiliary processes except startup, syslogger and stats collector, and background workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected that the docs would then repeat the same list of exceptions every time they mention a crash. He suggested documenting in one central place which conditions start a crash-and-restart cycle. Daniel Gustafsson accepted this and proposed closing the entry as rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It seems to me that it will result in a lot of
duplication in the docs, because every time we talk about something
that happens in connection with a crash, we'll need to talk about this
same list of exceptions.

precedents_retrieved.title: LockHasWaiters() crashes on fast-path locks
precedents_retrieved.summary: LockHasWaiters() dereferences NULL lock and proclock pointers when the LOCALLOCK was taken via the fast path, which crashes for weak lock modes such as AccessShareLock. Early versions moved the lock into the main lock table first; v4 instead searches LockMethodProcLockHash and returns false when no entry exists.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier saw no reason to support the case on its own, because no core caller or test needs it; the only existing caller uses AccessExclusiveLock, which is never fast-pathed. He suggested an assert and a comment instead, and said the patch looks like dead code without the separate autoprewarm proposal that needs it. Bharath Rupireddy withdrew the entry and moved the patch into the autoprewarm thread as 0001.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see a strong need to support this case if we have nothing in core to test it and nothing in core that needs it, and there are no facts that we need to do anything.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add function - pg_accept_connections_start_time()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a SQL function, renamed in v2 to pg_postmaster_open_time(), that returns the time the server last became ready to accept connections. Unlike pg_postmaster_start_time(), the value resets after crash recovery without a postmaster restart, so uptime and server restarts can be measured more accurately.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show an explicit rejection. The last message is Fujii Masao's review of v2, which asks the author to document that the timestamp changes when a standby is promoted. No reply or new patch version appears between that message on 2025-03-06 and the return on 2025-07-25. Tom Lane objected only to the side idea of extending postmaster.pid for pg_ctl status, not to the function itself.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
Reverted commit(s): Add redo LSN to pgstats files
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit b860848232aa, that was added as a prerequisite for
the support of pgstats data flush across checkpoints, linking a pgstats
file to a specific checkpoint redo LSN.

As reported, this is proving to be currently problematic when going
through a pg_upgrade, that does direct manipulations of the control file
in the new cluster.  The LSN stored in the pgstats file is not able to
cope with any changes done in the control file by pg_upgrade yet,
causing the pgstats file to be discarded when starting the new cluster
after overriding its redo LSN (one is a `pg_resetwal -l` where the new
cluster's start LSN is bumped by a hardcoded value of 8 segments, see
copy_xact_xlog_xid).

The least painful path going forward is likely going to be a refactor of
the pgstats code so as it is possible to read and write some of its data
with some routines in src/common/, so as pg_upgrade or pg_resetwal are
able to update its data.  The main point is that we are going to need a
LSN in the stats file should we make it written at checkpoint time and
not only as part of a shutdown sequence.  It is too late to dive into
these details for v18, so let's revert the change, and let's try to
figure out all the details in the next release cycle.  The pgstats file
is currently only written as part of a shutdown sequence, and its
contents are still lost on crash, same as older releases.

Bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: skip replication slot snapshot/map file removal during end-of-recovery checkpoint
precedents_retrieved.summary: Skip the enumeration and removal of logical replication snapshot (.snap) and mapping (map-) files during the end-of-recovery checkpoint, so the server becomes available sooner, and leave the files to the next regular checkpoint. A GUC could control this, with the current behavior as the default.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Nathan Bossart argued that skipping the files only at end of recovery does not solve the problem, because regular checkpoints stay slow and the shutdown or end-of-recovery checkpoint can still take a long time. He proposed moving these tasks out of checkpointing, which another thread was already discussing. The author agreed to handle the problem in that thread and withdrew this entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If
there are frequently many such files to delete and regular checkpoints
are taking longer, the shutdown/end-of-recovery checkpoint could still
take a while.  I think it would be better to separate these tasks from
checkpointing instead.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recovery prefetching feature.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recovery prefetching feature.
Reverted commit(s): Doc: Review for "Optionally prefetch referenced data in recovery."; Optionally prefetch referenced data in recovery.; Add circular WAL decoding buffer.; Remove read_page callback from XLogReader.; Sync guc.c and postgresql.conf.sample with the SGML docs.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This set of commits has some bugs with known fixes, but at this late
stage in the release cycle it seems best to revert and resubmit next
time, along with some new automated test coverage for this whole area.

Commits reverted:

dc88460c: Doc: Review for "Optionally prefetch referenced data in recovery."
1d257577: Optionally prefetch referenced data in recovery.
f003d9f8: Add circular WAL decoding buffer.
323cbe7c: Remove read_page callback from XLogReader.

Remove the new GUC group WAL_RECOVERY recently added by a55a9847, as the
corresponding section of config.sgml is now reverted.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use fadvise in wal replay
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the startup process call posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED) on WAL segment files during replay, prefetching a fixed 128kB chunk ahead of the current read position. It targets standbys where OS readahead is disabled and the startup process spends its time waiting on WAL reads from disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks by Tomas Vondra showed the patch helps only when OS readahead is disabled, and he saw no good reason to run that way. Andres Freund added that systems without useful readahead also lack posix_fadvise, and a hardcoded 128kB distance is too short for cases such as cloud storage. The CFM marked it Returned with feedback and suggested starting over with a different approach.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's not going to help OSs
without useful readahead, because those don't have posix_fadvise either. And
hardcoded readahead distance isn't useful - on e.g. cloud storage 128kB won't
be long enough to overcome network latency.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add DB_IN_END_OF_RECOVERY_CHECKPOINT state for control file
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stops the end-of-recovery checkpoint from setting the control file state to DB_SHUTDOWNING and then DB_SHUTDOWNED, which the author considered wrong. Two variants were posted: one adds a new state DB_IN_END_OF_RECOVERY_CHECKPOINT, and one keeps DB_IN_CRASH_RECOVERY or DB_IN_ARCHIVE_RECOVERY until DB_IN_PRODUCTION.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier argued that the current state is not incorrect, because an end-of-recovery checkpoint is a shutdown checkpoint and the code has relied on that for about 10 years. He said the change was not checked against other assumptions, such as unlogged relation reset needing a clean shutdown, and that it leaves an invalid minimum recovery point in DB_IN_ARCHIVE_RECOVERY. He added that it would make back-patching harder in a sensitive area, and the entry was closed after the thread went quiet.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This
patch would bring some extra visibility for something that's not
incorrect either on HEAD, as end-of-recovery checkpoints are the same
things as shutdown checkpoints.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent proposes on-demand page redo after crash recovery. The two objections rest on reasons from related attempts that still apply.
Not applicable: three objections from the standards and compatibility angle.
No on-disk format, catalog or wire protocol change is proposed. The objections concern WAL retention, crash restarts and replication tooling during the pending window.

The proposal grants no new privilege and exposes no data, query text or file access to non-superusers; the GUC is server-start only and off by default, and replay sits below the RLS and permission layer. Not checkable without code: whether an unprivileged session can delay a hot page's replay for other readers by cancelling it repeatedly with statement_timeout.
Objections were found; see the list.
No extension or external tool does on-demand per-page redo. Both objections concern existing ways to reduce part of the downtime.
Two demand objections raised; both are "show demand" in kind, not proof that the idea lacks users.
